title: Culture and Experience Shape Emotions
keyIdea: The same event can make different people feel different things. Between the event and the feeling sits a thought about what the event means, which psychologists call an appraisal. Past experiences shape that thought: a child once bitten by a dog may think 'it will bite me' and feel scared, while a child who grew up with a dog feels delighted. Cultural background and family norms shape it too, including display rules about which feelings to show in public. Knowing this helps us respond with empathy instead of judging someone's feeling as wrong.

kid: Picture a thunderstorm. Ava hides under a blanket, Jo runs to the window grinning, and Sam keeps reading his book. It is one storm, yet there are three different feelings. So the storm alone cannot decide how someone feels.

Something sits in the middle: a thought about what the event means. If you think 'this could hurt me', you feel scared. If you think 'this is exciting', you feel thrilled. Psychologists call this quick thought an appraisal. The order goes event, then thought, then feeling.

Your past shapes that thought. Ava once saw a storm blow a tree onto her roof, so thunder brings back danger. Jo counts the seconds to the thunder with her grandad, so storms mean fun. Your past teaches your brain what to expect.

Your family and culture shape it too. In some homes, being praised in front of everyone feels wonderful. In other homes, standing out feels like showing off, so the same praise brings embarrassment. When a friend feels differently from you, ask about it kindly. Their feeling makes sense from where they stand.
adult: This lesson teaches appraisal. The idea comes from the psychologist Richard Lazarus. A feeling comes from how we read an event, not from the event itself. Children aged 9 to 11 can use a simple chain: trigger, then thought, then feeling. It helps them see why friends react in different ways to the same storm, test or dog.

Two things shape the thought. The first is past experience. A scary time with a dog makes the next dog seem a threat. Safe, happy time with dogs makes them seem friendly. The second is cultural background. Families and cultures differ in what they value. They also have display rules: shared habits about which feelings to show, to whom and how much. Praise in public and talk about money are two places where these habits differ.

A common misconception is that a feeling is wrong, or an overreaction, when it differs from ours. Another slip is the stereotype that everyone from one culture feels the same. Be careful here. Treat culture as one influence among many, and say that people differ inside every family. Do not use real countries as examples.

The lab ends with perspective-taking and empathy. Learners sort replies to a scared friend. Some replies name the feeling and offer help; others brush it aside. This links to the RSHE mental wellbeing goals on noticing and talking about feelings. It also links to the CASEL skill of social awareness: seeing things from the point of view of people from other backgrounds.

familyTip: Share a time when you and a relative felt differently about the same event, such as a fairground ride, a spider or a family party. Talk about what each person thought it meant and what in their past or upbringing might explain that thought. Then ask your learner for an example of their own.

visual.caption: Is it the event or the thought about it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A dog runs up to you
Your name is read out in assembly
A friend asks what your shoes cost

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match pasts to feelings, put a thought between event and feeling, slide Mia's past, predict pride or embarrassment, and sort kind replies.

practice.prompt: Max and Lily both hear a firework bang. Max cheers and Lily covers her ears. What best explains the difference?
choices: Each one has a different thought about what the bang means
The firework was louder for Lily
practice.hint: The bang is the same for both. What happens inside each head?
practice.explain: The event is the same. Each child's thought about it (fun or danger) leads to a different feeling.

practice.prompt: {n} children watch the same scary film. Each one has a different past, and each one has their own thought about the film. How many thoughts are there?
practice.hint: Count one thought for every child watching.
practice.explain: {=n} children make {=n} thoughts. One film can lead to {=n} different feelings, because each thought comes from a different past.

practice.prompt: Kai feels embarrassed when he is praised in front of the whole school. At home, quiet praise is the norm. What shaped his feeling?
choices: His family's norms about standing out
He did not deserve the praise
practice.hint: Think about what Kai has learned at home about being noticed.
practice.explain: Family and cultural norms taught Kai that standing out can look like showing off, so his thought is 'everyone is staring' and he feels embarrassed.

practice.prompt: In a class of {a} children, {b} feel excited about a trip to the farm. Everyone else feels nervous. How many feel nervous?
practice.hint: Take the excited children away from the whole class.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} leaves {=a-b} nervous children. Same trip, two kinds of feeling, and both make sense.

pool.prompt: What comes between an event and a feeling?
choices: A thought about what the event means
pool.hint: Remember the chain: event, then something, then feeling.
pool.explain: The chain is event, thought, feeling. The thought, or appraisal, is why one event can bring different feelings.

pool.prompt: Nia was bitten by a dog when she was five. Now she freezes when a puppy runs up. Which word explains this best?
pool.hint: Think about something that happened to Nia before.
pool.explain: Her past taught her to expect a bite, so her thought is 'it will hurt me' and her feeling is fear.

pool.prompt: Your friend is scared of a small, friendly dog. Which reply shows empathy?
choices: "That looks scary for you. Shall we cross over?"
pool.hint: Which reply names the feeling and offers help?
pool.explain: Empathy means seeing it from their side. Naming the feeling and offering help shows you take it seriously.

choices: "Everyone from that country hates being praised."
"People can feel differently about the same event."
pool.hint: Look for a sentence that says everyone in a group feels the same.
pool.explain: A stereotype claims a whole group is the same. Real families and people vary, even within one culture.

pool.prompt: Ben feels uneasy when a friend asks loudly what his trainers cost. At home, money is a private topic. What is happening?
choices: His family's norms shape his thought, so he feels uneasy
pool.hint: What has Ben learned at home about money?
pool.explain: In Ben's family money is private, so a loud question feels like a rule broken. His feeling is uneasy.

pool.prompt: {n} friends ride the same roller coaster. {k} of them loved it and the rest felt sick with fear. How many felt fear?
pool.hint: Take the ones who loved it away from all the friends.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} leaves {=n-k}. The ride was the same; the thoughts and pasts were different.

pool.prompt: A lab card has 3 parts: event, thought and feeling. You fill in {n} cards. How many parts do you write?
pool.hint: Each card has the same 3 parts. Multiply.
pool.explain: {n} cards with 3 parts each is {=3*n} parts. Always put the thought between the event and the feeling.

choices: Shared norms about which feelings to show, and when
Rules saying which feelings are wrong
pool.hint: They come from family and culture, and they are about showing feelings.
pool.explain: Display rules guide which feelings are shown in public. They differ between families and cultures.
